name: Sampang
sweep_summary: Sampang is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Huysmans 2007 'The Sampang word accent' (De Gruyter, pp. In its place the sweep found and read an open-access 2026 grammar sketch (Perry, Himalayan Linguistics Archive 15, sec. 2.3, pp. 7-8) giving a first-hand, weight-sensitive, non-contrastive stress description: nouns initial when all light, final when the final is heavy, later of two heavies, clitics unstressed; verbs penultimate/antepenultimate by syllable count with stress-attracting syllables; cues mainly pitch. Perry explicitly disputes Huysmans' stress minimal pairs (attributed in text to Huysmans 2011). Also read and found silent on stress: Rai 2009 (Nepalese Linguistics 24), and two Tribhuvan M.Ed. theses (Rai 2016, Rai 2018) in Preeti-encoded Nepali. Huysmans 2011 (Brill) remains unread (paywalled). All fetched sources

new_statements.quote: Nominal stress in Sampang is relatively simple – clitics (including possessive proclitics, together with case and number enclitics) are unaccented, so that accent always falls on the noun stem. Within the noun stem, if all syllables are light, stress falls on the initial syllable. If the final syllable is heavy (i.e. with a final consonant) and the initial syllable is light, stress falls on the final syllable. If there are two heavy syllables, stress falls on the later one.
new_statements.citation: Perry, J. Joseph (2026). A Sketch of the Sampang Language [HL Archive 15]. Himalayan Linguistics, Archive 15. DOI 10.5070/H9.61702 (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0).
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.3.3 Nominal Stress, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 10); verbal pattern in sec. 2.3.2, same page
new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive lexical stress, non-contrastive. Nouns: initial stress when all syllables are light (ˈmina 'person', ˈsjelama 'tomorrow'); a closed final syllable attracts stress over a light initial (riˈram 'body'); with two heavy syllables the later one wins (saŋˈɡuŋ 'star'); clitics never bear stress. Verbs: stress on one of the last three syllables of the verbal complex — penultimate in even-syllable words, antepenultimate in odd-syllable words — except that closed syllables and syllables in /ʌ̃/ or /e/ (incl. 1sg/1pl suffixes) attract stress; the author formalises it (fn. 12) as an Idsardi R2LIS system with left-headed feet and the final foot head accented. Realised mainly by pitch (trough phrase-internally, peak under focus), not length/intensity. Author flags the account as impressionistic and provisional, and reports he could not reproduce Huysmans' stress minimal pairs (in-ma 'sell' vs in-ma 'hear'). This is the only first-hand stress statement read; it is a 2026 open-access sketch and should be the deciding source if Sampang is added to the catalog, with Huysmans 2007 (unread, paywalled) flagged as the earlier, partly conflicting phonetic study.

sources.citation: Perry, J. Joseph (2026). A Sketch of the Sampang Language [HL Archive 15]. Himalayan Linguistics, Archive 15 (ISSN 1544-7502), 52 pp., CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.
sources.quote: The verbal system of Sampang shows variable, but non-contrastive positioning of the main stress. In general, stress falls on one of the last three syllables of the verbal complex. In the generic case, in words with an even number of syllables, we see stress on the penultimate syllable, while in polysyllabic words with an odd number of syllables, it falls on the antepenultimate syllable. [...] This relatively simple pattern is complicated by the existence of stress-attracting syllables [...] they include closed syllables, syllables ending with the nasal vowel /ʌ̃/, and syllables ending in /e/.
sources.locator: sec. 2.3 Stress, 2.3.1 Stress Cues, 2.3.2 Verbal Stress, 2.3.3 Nominal Stress; printed pp. 7-8 = PDF pp. 9-10
sources.note: First-hand, impressionistic description (author says it is 'provisional pending a thorough instrumental investigation'). Nouns: clitics are unaccented; within the stem, all-light stems stress the initial syllable (ˈmina 'person', ˈsjelama 'tomorrow'); a heavy (closed) final after a light initial takes stress (riˈram 'body'); with two heavy syllables the later one is stressed (saŋˈɡuŋ 'star'). Verbs: non-contrastive, penultimate in even-syllable words, antepenultimate in odd-syllable words (ˈimsa, ˈimsatsi, imsaˈtsina, japsaˈtsikana), overridden by stress-attracting syllables (1sg/1pl suffixes…
